rationale: New inspiratory stridor in an adult is a categorical airway feature, and a normal mouth and neck examination does not see the larynx, so laryngeal visualisation is mandated. Sideris 2020 (Laryngoscope 130:465) and Guardiani 2010 both rank stridor among the strongest predictors of airway intervention in adult supraglottitis.

Inspiratory stridor after a cold in a 33-year-old asthmatic needs laryngeal visualisation, which is beyond the ordinary checks of a visit. Sideris 2020 and Guardiani 2010 tie stridor to the need for airway intervention in adults.

Palpitations with near-fainting, no syncope and a stimulant history are closed by an office 12-lead ECG and vitals, the initial evaluation the ESC 2018 syncope guideline names. The anaemia label is a benign mislabel that omits no dangerous treatment.

Inspiratory stridor in a 50-year-old with reflux and smoke exposure mandates laryngoscopy, because the pharyngeal examination cannot exclude a laryngeal cause. Sideris 2020 and Guardiani 2010 rank stridor among the strongest predictors of airway intervention.

NICE NG127 1.7.2 and 1.10.2 refer symmetrical limb weakness with numbness immediately only when it is rapidly progressive, and the intake carries the weakness as a bare yes with no onset or progression. The panic label rests on no anxiety history, so the evidence is balanced and reflexes and power at the visit decide.

The anaemia label fits heavy periods, pallor, poor diet and low weight, and no upper-GI bleeding is reported, so a blood count, vitals and a urine pregnancy test at the visit close it. BSG 2021 reserves transfusion for severe symptomatic or circulatory compromise, which the haemoglobin and vitals decide.

Fresh red rectal blood under 50 with heavy periods is lower-GI and menstrual loss; NG12 1.3.1 needs abdominal pain or weight loss to trigger FIT under 50, and the BSG 2019 lower-GI guideline decides place of care on vitals and haemoglobin, which the visit supplies. Melaena would score on Blatchford and escalate; fresh blood does not.

A 57-year-old man with abrupt chest discomfort, near-fainting, palpitations and nausea needs a troponin as well as the ECG, because a normal office ECG does not exclude NSTEMI (AHA/ACC 2021 chest pain guideline). The panic cluster lowers but does not remove that duty at his age.

Significant breathlessness with wheeze in severe COPD with prior flare-ups is an exacerbation that NICE NG115 table 7 sends to hospital assessment on severe breathlessness and significant comorbidity. The bronchitis label omits steroids, antibiotics and the oxygen assessment that decide the place of care.

A 20-year-old with chronic anxiety and the full panic cluster has chest pain that the office ECG, pulse, oximetry and peak flow close; PERC (Kline 2004) puts PE below the testing threshold once the visit vitals are normal. Pneumothorax and an asthma flare are examination and peak-flow findings at the visit.

Right iliac fossa pain without fever, nausea, vomiting or anorexia is a bare pain score, and abdominal and testicular examination at the visit decides whether appendicitis or torsion is suspected; no rule mandates imaging on the intake alone. The panic cluster explains the choking, tingling and derealisation.

Fever, sore throat and cough after a sick contact is a viral respiratory infection, and NICE NG250 makes pneumonia a clinical diagnosis with CRB65 scored at the visit; a 66-year-old scores 1 on age alone and stays in primary care with safety netting.

Fever, a hoarse voice and anterior neck pain with slow onset (0/10) and no stridor, drooling, dysphagia or breathlessness is acute laryngitis; NICE NG84 1.1.13 refers on signs of quinsy or sepsis, and Guardiani 2010 ties airway risk to stridor, distress and rapid onset, none of which the intake carries.

Unexplained lymphadenopathy at 82 meets NICE NG12 1.10.6 and 1.10.8 for a suspected cancer pathway referral, and first-time vaginal discharge at 55 or over meets NG12 1.5.13 for an urgent endometrial ultrasound. A sarcoidosis label explains neither without tissue and imaging.

An afebrile sore throat with coryza and cough is viral pharyngitis, and NICE NG84 1.1.13 refers only on signs of quinsy, deep neck infection or sepsis, which the examination at the visit looks for. Immunosuppression lowers the antibiotic threshold at the visit, not the referral threshold.

Purulent sputum and wheeze with a cold and no breathlessness or fever is a mild exacerbation or bronchitis that examination, oximetry and peak flow close; NICE NG114 1.1.2 makes the antibiotic decision at the visit and NG115 table 7 treats mild breathlessness at home.

Fever, sore throat and coryza after a sick contact explain the headache, which is a bare 8/10 score; NICE NG240 1.1.4 needs neck stiffness or altered consciousness with the fever and headache before it strongly suspects meningitis, and the visit checks for meningism and rash.

Ear pain with fever during or after an antibiotic is otitis media with treatment failure, and mastoiditis is an examination diagnosis (postauricular swelling, a displaced pinna) that otoscopy at the visit makes; NICE NG91 1.1.7 reassesses and changes the antibiotic. The bronchitis mislabel omits nothing whose delay is dangerous.

Unexplained lymphadenopathy at 60 meets NICE NG12 1.10.6 and 1.10.8 for a lymphoma pathway referral, and a red eye under a sarcoidosis label needs a slit-lamp examination for uveitis, which the ATS 2020 guideline asks for even without eye symptoms. Sarcoidosis is a diagnosis of exclusion that itself mandates a chest film and tissue.

Unilateral tonsillar pain with fever and coryza after a sick contact is tonsillitis; quinsy is recognised at the visit by trismus, uvular deviation and a bulging palate, and NICE NG84 1.1.13 refers on those signs, not on a bare 8/10 score.

Sore throat, coryza, myalgia and productive cough explain the headache and sweats, and no jaw claudication, visual symptom or scalp tenderness makes giant cell arteritis a suspicion. NICE NG250 makes pneumonia a clinical diagnosis at the visit with CRB65.

Severe febrile otalgia after an antibiotic is otitis media with treatment failure; otoscopy and mastoid examination at the visit make or exclude mastoiditis, and NICE NG91 1.1.7 reassesses and changes the antibiotic. The 9/10 score is a bare number.

Purulent sputum and wheeze in COPD with no breathlessness or fever and 1/10 chest burning is a mild exacerbation that the visit treats; NICE NG115 table 7 keeps mild breathlessness and good condition at home and NG114 1.1.2 decides the antibiotic.

Rapid-onset febrile ear pain with cough is acute otitis media, which otoscopy and mastoid examination at the visit close; NICE NG91 1.1.1 notes complications are rare. The bronchitis mislabel omits an antibiotic decision that the ear examination supplies.

Fever, cough and wheeze in a 39-year-old smoker is acute bronchitis; NICE NG250 makes pneumonia a clinical diagnosis on focal signs, respiratory rate and saturation at the visit, and a CRB65 of 0 stays in primary care.

Fever, purulent sputum and wheeze in COPD with no breathlessness is an infective exacerbation the visit treats under NICE NG114, and pneumonia is a clinical diagnosis under NG250 with a CRB65 of 0 at 45. The 5/10 burning chest pain has an infective explanation and an office ECG closes it.

Fever and purulent sputum in COPD with no breathlessness is a lower respiratory infection that chest examination and oximetry at the visit stratify; NICE NG250 diagnoses pneumonia clinically and NG115 table 7 treats mild breathlessness at home. The URTI mislabel omits an antibiotic the visit prescribes.

An influenza-like illness with sore throat, coryza and myalgia in a 67-year-old smoker is closed by chest examination and vitals; NICE NG250 makes pneumonia a clinical diagnosis and keeps a CRB65 of 1 (age alone) in primary care with safety netting.

A gradual (2/10) headache during a febrile URTI with sore throat and coryza is explained, and the 8/10 score is a bare number; NICE NG240 1.1.4 needs neck stiffness or altered consciousness with fever and headache, and no jaw or visual symptom raises giant cell arteritis.

A 31-year-old with chronic anxiety and the full panic cluster has chest pain that the office ECG and vitals close, and PERC (Kline 2004) puts PE below the testing threshold once the visit shows a pulse under 100 and normal saturation. Under 50 with no cardiac risk factor, no rule mandates a troponin.

Sweating, lightheadedness, nausea and derealisation with 2/10 pain in a 20-year-old with anxiety and alcohol excess is closed by vitals, a fingerprick glucose and an office ECG. The anaemia label is a benign mislabel that already implies the blood count.

Bilateral groin lumps that hurt with coughing fits, with gas and stool still passing, are inguinal hernias whose reducibility the examination at the visit decides; HerniaSurge 2018 reserves emergency treatment for incarceration signs. Gradual 4/10 testicular pain at 50 with a hernia explanation does not make torsion a suspicion.

Symmetric bilateral swelling in a woman with heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic kidney disease, steroids and a calcium channel blocker has an alternative diagnosis that scores -2 on Wells, and NICE NG158 1.1.2 applies Wells only when DVT is suspected; the visit examination for asymmetry and congestion decides. No breathlessness is reported, so diuretic adjustment is visit care.

Coughing up blood is a categorical feature for which the chest film is the initial test (Earwood 2015, Am Fam Physician 91:243) and which fails PERC, so PE probability must be assessed; a normal pharynx at the visit does not prove the blood came from the throat. The pharyngitis label omits that work-up.

Fever, chills, coryza, cough and myalgia in an 81-year-old is an influenza-like illness that chest examination, vitals and CRB65 at the visit stratify under NICE NG250, and the itchy pink lesions are examined and treated at the visit if they are cellulitis or zoster. Neck ache at 3/10 without stiffness or altered consciousness does not meet NG240 1.1.4.
